claims.text: The Enabling Act of 1933 was passed by the Reichstag on 23 March 1933 with a vote of 444 to 94. Only the Social Democratic Party (SPD) voted in opposition to the Enabling Act of 1933. The Communist delegates had been banned from participation in politics and were absent during the vote on the Enabling Act of 1933. The Nazis and their ally the DNVP did not have the two-thirds majority required for the constitutional amendment on their own. The Nazis and their ally the DNVP obtained the two-thirds majority required for the constitutional amendment through intimidation of deputies. The Nazis and their ally the DNVP surrounded the Reichstag with SA members as part of their intimidation tactics. The Nazis and their ally the DNVP promised religious freedom protections to the Catholic Centre Party to obtain the two-thirds majority required for the constitutional amendment. The Reichstag president Hermann Göring changed the rules of procedure to reduce the quorum needed to call up a law amending the constitution from two-thirds of the entire Reichstag membership (432 deputies) to 378. Hermann Göring reduced the quorum needed to call up a law amending the constitution by not counting the 81 absent Communist deputies. The government had arrested all Communist and some Social Democrat deputies under the Reichstag Fire Decree. The conservative parties representing the middle class, Junkers, and business interests were expected to vote for the Enabling Act of 1933. The Nazis used a strategy of coercion, bribery, and manipulation of parliamentarians to secure the Enabling Act of 1933's passage.
claims.reason: "When the newly-elected Reichstag convenednot including the Communist delegates whose participation in politics had been bannedit passed the Enabling Act (23 March 1933)." - vote 444 to 94, only SPD opposed, Communists banned and absent, Nazis and DNVP lacked two-thirds but obtained it through intimidation including SA surrounding Reichstag and promises to Catholic Centre Party; Hermann Göring changed quorum rules reducing it from 432 to 378 by excluding 81 absent Communists; government arrested Communists and some Social Democrats; conservatives expected to support; Nazis used coercion, bribery, manipulation.

claims.text: Mussolini's March on Rome in October 1922 was an organized mass demonstration of fewer than 30,000 men. Mussolini's March on Rome led to King Victor Emmanuel III handing power to Mussolini without armed conflict. King Victor Emmanuel III feared civil war. King Victor Emmanuel III persuaded the then Prime Minister Luigi Facta to resign. King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini as Prime Minister. The appointment of Mussolini as Prime Minister transferred power legally within the framework of the Italian constitution (Statuto Albertino). Mussolini's March on Rome was not a seizure of power but a precipitating force behind a constitutional transfer of power. The constitutional transfer of power was made possible by the surrender of public authorities in the face of fascist intimidation. Hitler's attempt to emulate Mussolini's March on Rome with a "March on Berlin" resulted in the failed Beer Hall Putsch in 1923. Mussolini did not respond to Hitler's requests for guidance on organizing a march. Mussolini showed little interest in Hitler's movement. The sources do not cover the details of how Hitler actually became chancellor in 1933. The sources only state that Hitler's attempted march on Berlin failed in 1923.

claims.text: The Nazis took apart the working democracy of the Weimar Republic in a matter of months by using the powers granted to Hitler as Chancellor to thwart constitutional governance and suspend civil liberties. This led to the swift collapse of democracy and the creation of a one-party dictatorship under Hitler's leadership. Hitler was sworn in as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Hitler asked President Paul von Hindenburg to dissolve the Reichstag and call new elections for 5 March 1933. During the election campaign, the Nazis claimed Germany was on the verge of a communist revolution. The Nazis argued that only Nazi power could stop the communist revolution. After the election, Hitler sought to abolish democracy quasi-legally by passing the Enabling Act. The Enabling Act gave Hitler the power to pass laws by decree without Reichstag involvement for four years. Within months, all other political parties were banned. The Nazi regime seized control of the media. The Nazi regime arrested tens of thousands of political opponents, especially communists. The Nazi regime set up extrajudicial imprisonment camps. The Nazis cracked down on social outsiders. The Nazis abolished collective bargaining. The Nazis froze wages. The Nazis granted business owners unprecedented control over their workforce in exchange for business support. This combination of legal manipulation, repression, and alliance with business interests dismantled the democratic system rapidly.
claims.reason: "Hitler promptly used these powers to thwart constitutional governance and suspend civil liberties, which brought about the swift collapse of democracy at the federal and state level, and the creation of a one-party dictatorship under his leadership." - all key points about dismantling democracy and dictatorship under Hitler are covered.
